paragraphs.text:
When light waves meet, their vibrations add, strengthening the light in some places and weakening it in others.
This interference does more than produce bright and dark patterns: it can help us measure things and improve optical instruments.

Coherent light waves have the same frequency and a stable phase difference, so the timing of their vibrations relative to each other does not change unpredictably.
Splitting the same beam along different paths and then bringing the parts together can preserve this relationship.

An instrument that uses interference for measurement is called an interferometer.
A change in optical path shifts the bright and dark fringes, allowing precise measurements of quantities such as the wavelength of light or the refractive index of a gas, as well as specialized tests.

**Surface Quality Inspection** turns very small variations in a surface into visible changes in fringes.
The source reports a testing precision of $\frac{1}{10}$ of a wavelength and describes this sensitivity as approximately $10^{-6}$ centimetres.

These are the source's reported sensitivity figures, not a universal conversion from a fraction of a wavelength to centimetres.
Such a conversion needs the testing wavelength, which this source passage does not specify.

Place the surface being tested close to a very smooth reference plane, leaving a thin, wedge-shaped air layer between them, as in Figure 201.
Light reflected from the surfaces on either side of this air layer comes from the same incident beam and overlaps to form interference fringes.

With flat surfaces, the air-layer thickness changes regularly along the wedge, producing regularly arranged fringes.
A bump or hollow changes the local layer thickness and the path difference of the reflected light, bending the fringes.
The source states that surface variations of $10^{-6}$ centimetres already cause noticeable bending.

**Antireflection Treatment** addresses reflection at optical-glass surfaces.
Camera lenses, projector lenses, periscopes, and similar instruments contain lenses and prisms, so light encounters many surfaces in succession.

The source describes camera lenses with more than $10$ reflecting surfaces and submarine periscopes with as many as $40$.
At normal incidence, each surface can reflect $5$ to $9\%$ of the incident energy, and repeated reflections reduce the light travelling forward.

In the instruments described by the source, only $10$ to $20\%$ of the incident energy sometimes passes through, leaving the image dim.
Reflection can also reduce image clarity.
Some light reflects repeatedly inside the instrument before emerging forwards, but no longer converges at the correct image position, becoming stray light that produces a veiling haze.

Reducing surface reflection allows more light to form a bright image and reduces interference from stray reflections.
This treatment is called antireflection treatment, or optical transmission enhancement.
It does not amplify light: it reduces the light that would otherwise be reflected back.

Antireflection treatment uses thin-film interference.
Coat the glass with a transparent film whose refractive index $n_{\text{膜}}$ is smaller than the glass index $n_{\text{玻}}$, and whose index is larger than that of air.

We will consider only normal incidence: light arriving perpendicular to the surface, as in Figure $202$.
The same incident beam produces reflections at the upper film surface and at the film-glass boundary, and these reflected waves can interfere when they meet.

Call the light reflected at the upper film surface wave $1$, and the light that returns after reflection at the lower surface wave $2$.
The lower reflection travels into the film and back, adding a geometrical distance of $2h$ at normal incidence, twice the film thickness.

This extra journey is inside the film, so we must compare it with the wavelength inside the film, not directly with the vacuum wavelength.
The film wavelength $\lambda_{\text{膜}}$ is the vacuum wavelength $\lambda$ multiplied by $\frac{1}{n_{\text{膜}}}$, because the frequency stays the same while the propagation speed decreases on entering the film.

Frequency is the number of vibrations per second.
When light crosses a stationary boundary between media, its frequency stays the same, although its speed and wavelength can change.
To compare the colours of single-frequency light, connect colour to frequency rather than comparing wavelengths measured in different media alone.
$\lambda_{\text{膜}}=\frac{\lambda}{n_{\text{膜}}}$

For wave $1$ and wave $2$ to weaken each other in the returning direction, their vibrations must oppose each other: when one vibrates in a particular direction, the other vibrates in the opposite direction.
Under the reflection conditions used here, an extra distance of $\frac{1}{2}$ of the wavelength inside the film establishes this opposing relationship①.

① The indices satisfy $n_{\text{空}}<n_{\text{膜}}$, $n_{\text{膜}}<n_{\text{玻}}$, so both reflections occur at a boundary approached from the lower-index medium towards the higher-index medium.
Each reflected wave undergoes a phase change of $\pi$ at its reflecting boundary, reversing its vibration.
$2h=\frac{\lambda}{2n_{\text{膜}}}$ (7.8)

Opposing phase alone is not enough: the amplitudes of the reflected waves also matter.
Equal amplitudes allow equally large, opposite vibrations to cancel completely.

Nearly equal amplitudes greatly reduce the reflection but leave a small remainder.
Film design therefore requires both a thickness that sets the relative phase and a refractive index that makes the reflected amplitudes as equal as possible.
The refractive-index relationship between neighbouring media determines the strength of reflection at their boundary, so choosing the film material is another essential condition.

White light contains different frequencies, and the same film cannot give the strongest reflection cancellation for every colour.
The required thickness in equation (7.8) depends on wavelength, so a film designed for a particular wavelength need not work equally well for another.

① The source footnote says: "In practice, the thickness of the film is an integer multiple of the wavelength. This is more convenient."
This source wording is retained without changing "integer multiple" to a different multiple.

Under this lesson's normal-incidence model and stated air, film, and glass index relationship, the "integer multiple" statement is not a usable rule for choosing an antireflection-film thickness.
Both reflections reverse the vibration in the same way, so a thickness that is an integer multiple of the in-film wavelength adds a whole number of wavelengths on the return journey and does not give the required opposing vibrations.

The usable rule here is the quarter-wavelength thickness measured inside the film, with the stated phase and amplitude conditions still required.
Using the footnote's statement would need a missing premise about which wavelength it means and what additional conditions apply, neither of which the source supplies.
The footnote also credits the industrial method of coating optical glass to the Soviet researchers I. V. Grebenshchikov, A. N. Terenin, and others.
$h=\frac{\lambda_{\text{绿}}}{4n_{\text{膜}}}$

For the green-light coating described in the source, reflection of red and violet light near the edges of the spectrum is not reduced as strongly as reflection of green light.
The proportions of colours in the remaining reflected light therefore change, and the lens surface can show a pale violet reflection.

This describes light reflected back rather than transmitted forwards;
it does not mean that the lens transmits only violet light.

The source also notes that even simple, inexpensive cameras can use antireflection-treated lenses.
Treating the ice cracks described in the source as thin layers requires very thin air gaps, suitable illumination, and reflected light from both sides that can overlap.

Coloured glints are a possible observation under these conditions, not a feature guaranteed for every fracture.
This thin-layer idea does not let us simply reuse the coating's thickness rule.
The source describes an observation, not a request to make cracks.

Light cancelling light means that the combined vibration becomes smaller in a particular direction, not that light energy is destroyed or that interference itself turns it into heat.
As with mechanical-wave interference, a dark region receives less energy because the distribution of energy flow has changed.
